<reason>PRO (Side B) built and kept a coherent comparative route: the least-secure households are non-savers, deductions structurally cannot reach them (regressive value, asset shifting), and auto-enrollment converts them at scale while the match makes even a low default beat zero. CON (Side A) landed real damage on the edges—escalation is outside the motion, the "leakage is security functioning" move was rightly punished as a taxed/penalized emergency fund, and the concession that opt-outs skew toward stressed workers was exploited well—but CON's core claim that anchoring and liquidity harms outweigh headcount gains was never quantified and was substantially neutralized by PRO's "engaged savers change defaults / squeezed households opt out" filter and the match arithmetic. CON's attempt to strip the match backfired when PRO pointed out an uncaptured match is worth nothing and auto-enrollment is what captures it. CON's salience turn in A1 was clever but strained, its A2 conceded the extensive-margin gap, and its Rebuttal 2 was clipped. PRO answered the pressure questions squarely and made the decision rule easier: when the household does nothing, only one policy acts.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 2/Closing on the employer match: CON tried to strip the match as "belonging to the plan," and PRO turned it—an uncaptured match is worth nothing, and auto-enrollment is precisely what unlocks it for workers who never file paperwork—converting CON's sharpest late move into support for the bare policy.</best_rebuttal>
